newsitem.title: UK: KPMG looks to shed grey image with movie roles.
newsitem.headline: KPMG looks to shed grey image with movie roles.

text.p: KPMG, one of the biggest accountancy and management consultancy firms in the world, is trying to shake off a dull image associated with the industry by getting into the movies.
The firm, which has offices in 142 countries, told Reuters on Tuesday it had signed a deal with a company that specialises in placing brand-name products on movie sets as props.
KPMG said the product placement specialist Environment Marketing had agreed to get the KPMG brand into 18 films in the next two years.
"Accountants are often labelled as boring and this our bid to prove we are not," said David Murrell, KPMG's chairman of international marketing.
Many major brands, including Reebok, Apple Computer Inc and Mercedes Benz, pay millions of dollars for their brands and products to appear in Hollywood movies, industry sources told Reuters.
In the last James Bond film "GoldenEye", Bond drove a BMW, wore an Omega watch and drank Smirnoff vodka -- the kind of product endorsement that makes many consumer-product manufacturers drool.

And in the United States, Universal Studios and Amblin Entertainment are reported to have raised $250 million in product placement and "cross promotion" of brands that appear in "Lost World", the sequel to "Jurassic Park" due for release this summer.
Cross promotion includes a practice where brandname-product manufacturers arrange for their products to appear on films and then they help promote the films.
Industry sources said the investment by KPMG, which is based in Amsterdam, was modest compared to what some companies pay to get their products onto movie sets.
It will pay up to $17,000 for its offices or branded products such as coffee mugs and umbrellas to feature in a film.

Environment Marketing's Alex Gulland has already signed a deal with the producers of Robert De Niro's latest movie called "Wag the Dog". In one scene De Niro will pass Dustin Hoffman a mug of coffee bearing the KPMG logo.
Gulland is also negotiating with the makers of "Critical Care" -- a new movie starring James Spader -- to get KPMG's name mentioned in an office scene.
In the UK, Gulland has persuaded Billy Herman, the producer of a low-budget romantic comedy called "The Sea Change", to make the hero an accountant who works at KPMG.

"The plot calls for the hero to be a wealthy professional. We could have made him a lawyer or an advertising executive but as KPMG were willing to invest in the film we have made him an accountant," Herman told Reuters.

Murrell said that KPMG is investing in product placement "because it will raise awareness of our name with the public. It will also boost internal morale -- four fifths of our staff are under 32 and therefore in that age group that goes to the cinema the most. It will be good for them to see the firm on screen".
Gulland said that another reason for the popularity of product placement is that it can have a longer life span than traditional advertising.

"A film gets rolled out around the world in an 18-month time frame and then it is released on video and cable and gets TV showings. It can be good value for money -- provided, that is, that the film is not a stinker," he said.
